text.content:
Every major threat has a stat block: what it rolls, how fast it moves in squares, how fast it escalates, and how to run it. When a creature acts against the crew, roll the listed pool and count 5+; that's what the crew is up against. The Creature Compendium holds each one as a threat actor — drop it on the map and roll its pools from its sheet, or pick it in the roll dialog's Opposed by list.

Escalation. An Escalation step names an Alert level, and Full Alert counts as every step at once — at a low Limit, a creature can go straight from asleep to hunting. A creature is active from the first Escalation step the Alert has reached — or from the start, if the heist says it is awake or aware — and stays active for the rest of the heist. It adds its +X at the end of every round the crew spends at its obstacle, and at every obstacle once it roams — or wherever it can hear the crew, if it hears a whole floor.

Opposed rolls. A creature that actively resists rolls its pool first; its Successes + 1 are your Difficulty. Its roll is just a count: it never Partials, Criticals or Botches. An NPC's check against a Difficulty (a Decoy, a snare) needs the full Difficulty.

Other threats in the ready-to-run heists use what's already here: the library cat is a House Cat; the librarian, restaurant staff and cleaning crew are Humans, at their Chapter 15 Difficulty; a rival crew is built like the players' spiders.

Spiders don't win fights with cats; they end them. Clear a creature's obstacle with its Weakness, Brawl or Intimidation and it backs off for the rest of that obstacle: no attacks, no +X there. If it roams, it's back at the next one, sulking.

A Weakness that shuts it in — a lid that's actually shut, a cloth over the cage — keeps it in for the rest of the heist: it can't leave, strike or hunt, and a covered animal sees nothing. A shut-in creature that can still see you through the glass still counts its +X at its own obstacle.

Engaged: a threat is engaged with you when it was already active and able to reach you this round, or when you're fighting it. If several engaged threats see you fail, the one with the biggest attack lands the hit.

Fights are loud: every roll of one that lands is +1 Alert, and a lost one is a Loud Failure.

“Ten Thousand Times Your Size.” Every human uses one block (the Human in the Creature Compendium): Threat Low (asleep) to High (broom); no Alert Contribution of its own; Speed 10; Swat 3; Perception 3 for its own checks only (a Decoy, a surprise).

  • You roll against its row. Sleeping, distracted, alert or armed with a broom — its Chapter 15 row sets your Difficulty. It never rolls to spot you.
  • Senses: sees anything in its room not in cover. A sleeper only hears.
  • Escalation: stirs at 5; up with the lights on at 7 or Full Alert. Its row stays the same.
  • Spotted and confirmed: a glimpse of a spider is “spotted” (+1); loot moving on its own is a confirmed alert (+2). One event, one trigger: a Failure that gets you spotted is +1, not +2.
  • Swatted: its reach is the room it's in: fail a roll there, where it can see you, and you're swatted (a hit, Swat 3). A Critical spider it hits ends up under a glass: Out.
  • Weakness: its phone, the TV, and a deep conviction that it imagined you.
ObstaclePrimary RollNotes
Sleeping HumanStealth (2)Asleep and fine — stay quiet. At Alert 5 they stir; at 7, or Full Alert, they're up and turning on lights.
Distracted HumanStealth (1)On their phone, watching TV. Use the window. It closes.
Alert HumanDeception or Stealth (4)Looking for something. Possibly for you. Do not get spotted.
Human With BroomAthletics (3)The broom has already swung once. Keep moving.

A threat with no attack pool — a broom, a snapping trap — rolls as many dice as its Chapter 15 Difficulty. When you roll to avoid a hazard, that roll decides whether it lands (a Failure is the hit); then you shrug.

Every active threat should have a patrol pattern or routine (mapped in squares), a trigger that flips it from passive to active, and an Alert reaction for the thresholds.

A loop isn't a timetable. At the end of each lap, roll 1d6: 1–2 it walks the lap backwards, 3–4 it rests a round, 5–6 it checks somewhere off its loop.

The clock. Waiting isn't free: when the crew starts a third round at one obstacle, roll a Mid-Heist Complication (Random Tables) — the world doesn't wait. Clock times in a heist (every ninety minutes, the cleaners at 8) arrive this way, or at a threshold; nobody converts rounds into minutes.

Lap roll: [[/gmr 1d6]]{Lap roll} · Mid-Heist Complication: [[/r 1d6]]{Complication}
